categoryDescriptions.popular: The ~200 chords used most in songs: 17 types × 12 roots. Each card shows the chord in [[root|root]] position: start on the root and stack the notes on top. Open a chord to see all its [[inversion|inversions]] and a two-hand voicing.
categoryDescriptions.triad: The basic three-note chords, or [[triad|triads]]. On the keys you skip one key each time: C – E – G on the white keys. [[major|Major]] (1–3–5) sounds bright, [[minor|minor]] (1–♭3–5) sad.
categoryDescriptions.sus: The 2nd (sus2) or 4th (sus4) [[degree|degree]] replaces the [[third|third]]. The chord is neither major nor minor, so it sounds suspended.
categoryDescriptions.sixth: A 6th or 9th is added to the [[triad|triad]], but there is no 7th.
categoryDescriptions.seventh: A 7th, the [[seventh|seventh]], goes on top of the triad. Four notes still fit comfortably in one hand. The core colour of jazz, blues and soul.
categoryDescriptions.extended: The 9th, 11th and 13th go on top of a [[seventhChord|seventh chord]]. Not every note fits in one hand, so pianists give the root (and the 7th) to the left hand and usually leave out the 5th.
categoryDescriptions.power: Just the [[root|root]] and [[fifth|fifth]] (1–5). On the piano it is used for an open, heavy bass in the left hand.
categoryDescriptions.slash: In a [[slashChord|slash chord]] (C/E) the left hand plays the note after the slash in the bass and the right hand plays the chord. It smooths out the bass line: C – G/B – Am.

voicings: Ways to play it on the keys
voicingsHint: Click a key to hear that note.

kindHints.close0: The root at the bottom. Start learning the chord here.
kindHints.close1: The lowest note moves up an octave, leaving the [[third|third]] in the bass.
kindHints.close2: The [[fifth|fifth]] in the bass. Your hand barely moves, so changes between chords are smooth.
kindHints.close3: The [[seventh|seventh]] in the bass. Only four-note chords have it.
kindHints.twoHands: The left hand gives the root in the bass, the right hand plays the rest. This is the voicing pianists use most.
kindHints.slash: The left hand plays the bass note, the right hand the chord in root position.

slashVersionsHint: The same chord with another chord tone in the bass. The left hand walks the bass line step by step.

scales.description: See a scale on the keys, hear it and learn its fingering. Major, natural minor and harmonic minor come with the standard fingering for both hands.
scales.fingerNames: 1 – thumb, 2 – index, 3 – middle, 4 – ring, 5 – little finger.
scales.fingeringHint: Going up, the right thumb passes under the hand, and in the left hand the 3rd or 4th finger crosses over the thumb. Those spots are highlighted. Coming down, use the same fingers in reverse.
scales.moreOctaves: For two octaves the right hand plays 1 instead of 5 on the top note and carries on; the left hand plays 1 instead of 5 on the bottom note.
scales.noFingering: This scale has no standard fingering. Pick major, natural minor or harmonic minor to see one.

builder.description: Build a chord yourself: pick a [[root|root]], then add or change the degrees one at a time. At every step the chord's name, notes, sound and place on the keys update right away.
builder.howToPlay: How to play it on the piano
builder.howToPlayHint: Big chords don't fit in one hand: the left hand gives the root in the bass, the right hand keeps the rest close together.
builder.noCatalog: This combination has no name in the catalogue. You can still see and hear its notes on the keys above.

fifth.none: You dropped the fifth. Pianists do it all the time in big chords: the fifth doesn't change the chord's name, it only adds body, and leaving it out frees a finger.

steps.4: A 9th instead of the 6th, no seventh: {{name}}. A favourite in pop and piano ballads.

styleHints.smooth: For each chord the right hand takes the [[inversion|inversion]] closest to the previous one: shared notes stay put, the rest step to the nearest key. This is how pianists play. The left hand gives the root in the bass.
styleHints.root: Every chord is in root position, so the hand jumps each time. Listen to both modes in turn and hear the difference.

progressions.first: The opening chord, in root position.
progressions.held_one: {{count}} note stays from the previous chord: {{notes}}.
progressions.held_other: {{count}} notes stay from the previous chord: {{notes}}.
progressions.noneHeld: No shared notes: the hand moves to a new place.
progressions.soloHint: Notes for right-hand improvising: the [[scale|scale]] ({{scale}}) in the background, the selected chord's own notes on top. While the left hand holds the chord, landing on the chord's notes is safest.

fingers.legend: The numbers under the keys are fingers: 1 – thumb, 2 – index, 3 – middle, 4 – ring, 5 – little finger. Dark numbers are the right hand, blue ones the left.
fingers.tooWide: This voicing doesn't fit in one hand, so it has no fingering. On the piano it is played with two hands — see the “Two hands” voicing.
fingers.towerTooWide: This tower doesn't fit in one hand. See the card beside it for how it is played on the piano.

intervals.description: Click any key and every [[interval|interval]] above it lights up in its colour. On the piano an interval is just a count of keys: any two neighbouring keys, white or black, are a semitone apart.
intervals.clickHint: Click another key to make it the new reference note.
intervals.lettersHint: An interval's number is the count of note letters: from C to E you pass C, D, E — three letters, a third. The semitones then say whether it is major, minor or perfect, which is why C–E♭ is also a third, just a minor one. The fingers are for playing both notes together.
